questions.stem: In which form does most of the Sun's energy reach Earth?
options: Long-wave infrared radiation emitted by the Sun's cool surface
Radio waves and microwaves produced in the Sun's outer layers
Gamma rays and X-rays that pass freely through the atmosphere
Visible light, with ultraviolet and near-infrared radiation
questions.explanation: The Sun's radiation peaks in the visible part of the spectrum, with significant ultraviolet and near-infrared. This short-wave radiation differs from the long-wave infrared that Earth emits.

questions.stem: Of the solar radiation arriving at the top of Earth's atmosphere, about what fraction is reflected straight back to space by clouds, air and the surface?
options: About 3%
About 70%
About 97%
About 30%
questions.explanation: Earth's overall albedo is about 0.3, so roughly 30% of incoming sunlight is reflected. The other 70% is absorbed by the atmosphere and surface.

questions.stem: On average over a year, a square metre of ground at the equator receives more solar energy than a square metre near the poles. Why?
options: The Sun's rays strike more directly, so the same energy falls on a smaller area
The equator is much closer to the Sun than the poles are, throughout the whole year
The equator has more ozone above it, which concentrates the incoming sunlight
The poles face away from the Sun permanently because of Earth's rotation
questions.explanation: Near the equator the Sun is high in the sky, so a beam of sunlight is concentrated on a small area. At high latitudes the same beam is spread over a larger area and passes through more atmosphere.

questions.stem: How does stratospheric ozone affect the solar radiation reaching Earth's surface?
options: It focuses ultraviolet radiation onto the surface, increasing the amount received
It absorbs most of the harmful ultraviolet radiation before it reaches the surface
It reflects most of the visible light back out to space before that light reaches the surface
It absorbs most of the infrared radiation emitted upward by Earth's surface
questions.explanation: Ozone impedes the transfer of ultraviolet radiation to the surface by absorbing it, which protects living things. Visible light passes through ozone largely unaffected.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes how ozone absorbs ultraviolet energy in the stratosphere?
options: UV splits O₂ into oxygen atoms, which join O₂ to form O₃; O₃ absorbs UV and splits again
UV joins two O₃ molecules into O₆, which then breaks down again to release infrared radiation
UV converts nitrogen into ozone, which then reflects the remaining UV back into space
UV splits O₃ into carbon dioxide and water, which then absorb the remaining sunlight
questions.explanation: Ozone is continually formed and broken down by ultraviolet radiation. Each step absorbs UV energy and converts it to heat, which is why the stratosphere warms with height.

questions.stem: Albedo is the:
options: proportion of incoming solar radiation that a surface absorbs
amount of infrared radiation a surface emits at night
amount of ozone in the atmosphere above a given surface
proportion of incoming solar radiation that a surface reflects
questions.explanation: Albedo ranges from 0, for a surface that absorbs everything, to 1, for a surface that reflects everything. It is a physical characteristic of Earth's surface that affects net energy transfer.

questions.stem: Which list ranks these surfaces from highest to lowest albedo?
options: Open ocean, forest, desert sand, fresh snow
Forest, fresh snow, open ocean, desert sand
Desert sand, open ocean, fresh snow, forest
Fresh snow, desert sand, forest, open ocean
questions.explanation: Fresh snow reflects most sunlight, sand reflects moderately, forest canopies absorb much of it, and the open ocean, seen from above, absorbs nearly all of it.

questions.stem: A surface receives 300 W per square metre of sunlight and has an albedo of 0.2. How much solar power does it absorb per square metre?
questions.explanation: Albedo 0.2 means 20% is reflected: 0.2 × 300 = 60 W. The rest, 300 − 60 = 240 W, is absorbed. Answering 60 W gives the reflected part.

questions.stem: A bushfire blackens a large area of pale, dry grassland. How does this change the energy balance of the surface?
options: Albedo is unchanged, because colour does not affect reflection
Albedo falls, so the surface absorbs less sunlight and cools more
Albedo falls, so the surface absorbs more sunlight and warms more
Albedo rises, so the surface reflects more sunlight and cools more
questions.explanation: Dark surfaces have low albedo. The blackened ground absorbs a larger share of incoming sunlight than the pale grass did, raising surface temperatures until vegetation regrows.

questions.stem: An area is half covered by snow (albedo 0.8) and half by forest (albedo 0.2). It receives 200 W per square metre of sunlight. How much does it absorb on average per square metre?
questions.explanation: The average albedo is (0.8 + 0.2) ÷ 2 = 0.5, so half the sunlight is absorbed: 0.5 × 200 = 100 W. If the snow melted and forest covered the whole area, absorption would rise to 160 W.

questions.stem: In which form does Earth's surface mainly emit energy?
options: X-rays and gamma rays
Infrared (long-wave) radiation
Ultraviolet (short-wave) radiation
Visible light, like the Sun
questions.explanation: Earth is much cooler than the Sun, so it emits mainly long-wave infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases interact with this outgoing infrared.

questions.stem: Which list contains only greenhouse gases?
options: Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide
Nitrogen, oxygen, argon and water vapour in equal parts
Nitrogen, carbon dioxide, oxygen and methane together
Oxygen, argon, helium and neon in the upper atmosphere
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation. Nitrogen and oxygen, which make up most of the air, and noble gases such as argon do not absorb it significantly.

questions.stem: How do greenhouse gases warm Earth's surface in the natural greenhouse effect?
options: They form a solid layer that stops any energy escaping from Earth into space
They absorb infrared radiation from the surface and send some of it back towards the surface
They absorb all the incoming visible sunlight and convert it directly into heat at the surface
They create heat chemically when they react with oxygen in the lower atmosphere
questions.explanation: Most thermal radiation from the surface eventually escapes to space, but greenhouse gases absorb some and re-emit it in all directions, including back down. This additional surface warming is the natural greenhouse effect.

questions.stem: Calculations suggest Earth's average surface temperature would be about −18 °C if its atmosphere had no greenhouse gases, compared with about 15 °C today. What does this comparison show?
options: The natural greenhouse effect is caused entirely by human emissions since 1800
The natural greenhouse effect has no effect on whether liquid water can exist
The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth about 33 °C warmer, allowing liquid water
The natural greenhouse effect cools Earth by about 33 °C, preventing the planet overheating
questions.explanation: The difference, about 33 °C, is the warming provided by naturally occurring greenhouse gases. Without it most of Earth's water would be frozen.

questions.stem: Why do greenhouse gases let most incoming sunlight pass through but absorb much of the radiation leaving Earth's surface?
options: Sunlight is mostly long-wave infrared, but Earth emits short-wave ultraviolet that they absorb
Greenhouse gases are found only near the ground, so they meet only the outgoing radiation
Incoming sunlight travels faster than outgoing radiation, so it passes before being absorbed
Sunlight is mostly short-wave, but Earth emits long-wave infrared that these gases absorb
questions.explanation: The hot Sun emits mainly short-wave radiation, which greenhouse gases barely absorb. The cool Earth emits long-wave infrared at wavelengths that molecules such as water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb strongly.

questions.stem: Which gas makes the largest contribution to the naturally occurring greenhouse effect?
options: Nitrogen
Argon
Water vapour
Oxygen
questions.explanation: Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas and contributes most to the natural greenhouse effect, followed by carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: The global ocean conveyor (thermohaline circulation) is driven mainly by differences in seawater:
options: colour, caused by differences in the amount of plankton
depth, caused by differences in the shape of the sea floor
tide height, caused by the Moon's changing gravitational pull
density, caused by differences in temperature and salinity
questions.explanation: Cold, salty water is denser and sinks, and it is replaced by water flowing in from elsewhere. Thermo refers to temperature and haline to salt.

questions.stem: Where does the dense deep water that drives the global ocean conveyor mainly form?
options: Along the equator, where warm, fresh water sinks under the trade winds
In the middle of large lakes, where fresh water mixes with river water
Around coral reefs, where reef-building animals add salt to the water
In the North Atlantic and around Antarctica, where cold, salty water sinks
questions.explanation: Surface water at high latitudes is chilled, and sea ice formation makes it saltier, so it becomes dense enough to sink to the ocean floor and spread through the deep ocean basins.

questions.stem: When sea ice forms around Antarctica, the water just beneath it becomes denser. Why?
options: Freezing releases oxygen into the water, and oxygen makes seawater much heavier
Sea ice blocks wind from the water, so it warms up and becomes denser below
Salt is left behind as seawater freezes, making the remaining water saltier and denser
Ice is denser than seawater, so it sinks and pushes the surrounding water down to the bottom
questions.explanation: Sea ice is mostly fresh water. Salt excluded during freezing increases the salinity of the cold water beneath, which then sinks as very dense bottom water.

questions.stem: How does the global ocean conveyor affect climate?
options: It carries heat from the tropics towards high latitudes, warming regions it reaches
It carries cold water to the tropics only, so it cools every part of the planet
It moves only deep water, so it has no effect on surface temperatures anywhere
It reverses direction every year, so its effect on climate always cancels out
questions.explanation: Warm surface currents carry tropical heat poleward while cold deep water returns towards the equator. For example, warm Atlantic water gives north-western Europe a milder climate than its latitude suggests.

questions.stem: What mainly drives surface ocean currents, and why do they form large circular gyres?
options: Tides drive them, and the shape of the Moon's orbit bends them into circles
Rivers drive them, and the flow of fresh water into the sea makes them circle
Undersea volcanoes drive them, and the heat from repeated eruptions makes the water spin around
Prevailing winds drive them, and Earth's rotation deflects them into circulating gyres
questions.explanation: Winds drag the surface water along, and the Coriolis effect from Earth's rotation deflects the moving water. Together with the continents this produces gyres, which turn anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.stem: The Leeuwin Current carries warm water southward along Western Australia's coast. Why is this unusual, and what is one effect?
options: Most currents flow only in deep water; it brings cold, nutrient-rich water up to the surface along the whole coast
Most currents are driven by tides; it reverses direction twice a day and so has no lasting effect on coastal waters
Most currents on oceans' eastern margins flow towards the equator and are cool; it lets tropical corals grow further south
Most currents on oceans' eastern margins flow towards the poles and are warm; it stops any corals growing off the coast
questions.explanation: Eastern boundary currents, such as the one off western South America, are usually cold and flow towards the equator. The warm, poleward Leeuwin Current allows coral reefs such as those of the Houtman Abrolhos to exist at unusually high latitudes.

questions.stem: The Leeuwin Current is typically stronger in La Niña years and weaker in El Niño years. What does this show?
options: Interactions between the Pacific Ocean and the atmosphere affect currents off Western Australia
The Leeuwin Current controls El Niño and La Niña, which both begin off the Western Australian coast
El Niño and La Niña affect only the Pacific, so the link must be a coincidence
The Leeuwin Current is driven by tides, which are stronger in La Niña years
questions.explanation: During La Niña, warm water piles up in the western Pacific and more flows through the Indonesian region into the Indian Ocean, strengthening the current. El Niño has the opposite effect.

questions.stem: Perth has a much smaller range between summer and winter temperatures than Kalgoorlie, which is inland. Why?
options: Kalgoorlie has more ozone above it, so it receives far more ultraviolet radiation in summer
Seawater's high heat capacity means the nearby ocean warms and cools slowly, moderating Perth
Perth is closer to the equator than Kalgoorlie, so it receives the same sunlight all year
The ocean produces its own heat in winter, which is carried inland only as far as Perth
questions.explanation: Water needs a lot of energy to change temperature, so the ocean stores heat in summer and releases it in winter. Coastal places therefore have milder summers and winters than inland places.

questions.stem: Unequal heating of Earth's surface sets up atmospheric circulation. What happens near the equator?
options: Warm air sinks, because heated air is denser than cool air
Warm air rises, creating low pressure, clouds and heavy rain
Cool air sinks, creating high pressure and clear, dry skies
Air stays still, because heating is equal in every direction
questions.explanation: Strong heating near the equator makes air expand and rise. As it rises it cools, so water vapour condenses into tall clouds and heavy rain, and low pressure forms at the surface.

questions.stem: In the three-cell model of atmospheric circulation, which cells lie in each hemisphere from the equator to the pole?
options: Hadley cell, Ferrel cell, polar cell
Polar cell, Hadley cell, Ferrel cell
Ferrel cell, polar cell, Hadley cell
Walker cell, Hadley cell, polar cell
questions.explanation: The Hadley cell runs from the equator to about 30°, the Ferrel cell from about 30° to 60°, and the polar cell from about 60° to the pole. The Walker circulation runs east-west across the Pacific.

questions.stem: Because of Earth's rotation, winds in the Southern Hemisphere are deflected:
options: to the left of their direction of motion
to the right of their direction of motion
straight towards the nearest pole
straight upward into the stratosphere
questions.explanation: The Coriolis effect deflects moving air to the left in the Southern Hemisphere and to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. This turns north-south flows into the trade winds and westerlies.

questions.stem: Air flowing at the surface from the subtropical high towards the equator in the Southern Hemisphere is deflected by Earth's rotation. Which winds result?
options: Westerly winds
Polar easterlies
South-east trade winds
North-west monsoon winds
questions.explanation: Air moving north towards the equator is deflected to the left, so it blows from the south-east. These steady south-east trades are part of the Hadley cell.

questions.stem: Perth has hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters. Which explanation based on atmospheric circulation is best?
options: The subtropical high-pressure belt lies over or south of Perth in summer, then moves north in winter, letting westerly cold fronts bring rain
The equatorial low-pressure belt lies over Perth in summer, then moves south in winter, bringing tropical storms and heavy monsoon rain to the south-west
The polar high-pressure belt lies over Perth all year, and winter rain comes from sea breezes that blow onshore every afternoon
The subtropical high-pressure belt lies over Perth all year, and winter rain comes from evaporation of the nearby Swan River
questions.explanation: Pressure belts shift with the seasons as Earth revolves around the Sun with its tilted axis. In winter the high-pressure belt moves north, so the westerlies and their cold fronts reach south-west Western Australia.

questions.stem: Many of the world's large hot deserts, including much of inland Australia, lie near 30° latitude. Why?
options: The Coriolis effect is strongest at 30°, which blows all clouds towards the poles
Dry air sinks in the subtropical high-pressure belt, warming and suppressing rain
Moist air rises in the subtropical low-pressure belt, raining before it reaches land
These latitudes receive the least sunlight on Earth, so no water can evaporate
questions.explanation: Air that rose at the equator and lost its moisture descends near 30°. Sinking air is compressed and warms, so clouds evaporate and rain is rare.

questions.stem: Northern Australia has a summer wet season. Which seasonal change in atmospheric circulation causes it?
options: The westerlies and their cold fronts shift north to reach the tropics in summer
The polar cell expands to the tropics, bringing cold moist air in summer
The monsoon trough and its zone of rising moist air move south over northern Australia
The subtropical high-pressure belt moves north over northern Australia during the summer
questions.explanation: As the Sun's most direct heating shifts south in the southern summer, the zone of rising air and heavy rain moves over northern Australia. In winter it moves back north and the dry season sets in.

questions.stem: In neutral conditions across the tropical Pacific, trade winds blow from east to west. What is the effect?
options: Cold water spreads across the whole Pacific, stopping all rainfall in Asia
The ocean surface stays still, because winds cannot move ocean water
Warm surface water piles up in the west, near Indonesia and northern Australia
Warm surface water piles up in the east, near the coast of South America
questions.explanation: The trade winds push warm surface water westward, where rising air brings rain. Off South America, cold, nutrient-rich water upwells to replace it. This east-west loop of air is the Walker circulation.

questions.stem: During an El Niño event, which change occurs in the tropical Pacific?
options: Trade winds stop permanently and the Walker circulation never returns to normal
Trade winds weaken and warm water spreads east, so eastern Australia tends to be drier
Trade winds strengthen and warm water builds in the west, so eastern Australia is wetter
Trade winds reverse to blow towards the poles, so the Pacific becomes colder everywhere
questions.explanation: As the trades weaken, the pool of warm water and the rising air shift towards the central and eastern Pacific. Air sinks more over Australia, so rainfall in eastern Australia is often below average.

questions.stem: Which description matches a La Niña event?
options: Stronger trade winds and warmer water near Australia, often bringing above-average rain to eastern Australia
Weaker trade winds and warmer water near South America, often bringing drought conditions to eastern Australia
Reversed trade winds and colder water near Australia, bringing snow to northern Australia
Normal trade winds and a cooler Indian Ocean, bringing no change at all to Australian rainfall
questions.explanation: La Niña is an enhanced version of normal conditions: stronger trades push more warm water west, strengthening rising air and rainfall over and near Australia.

questions.stem: The Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) is based on air pressure at Tahiti and Darwin. What does a sustained strongly negative SOI usually indicate?
options: A La Niña event
Neutral conditions
A cyclone in Perth
An El Niño event
questions.explanation: A strongly negative SOI means pressure is unusually high at Darwin relative to Tahiti, matching weaker trade winds and El Niño. Sustained positive values indicate La Niña.

questions.stem: Why did identifying El Niño and La Niña require systematic collection of air pressure and sea-surface temperature data over many decades?
options: The cycle affects only deep ocean water, so surface temperature and air pressure records are not needed at all
The cycle is irregular, recurring every few years over a whole ocean basin, so short local records cannot show it
The cycle happens every day at one location, so only hourly readings at a single station could reveal it
The cycle occurs only once a century, so one long record from a single ship was all that was needed
questions.explanation: ENSO events recur irregularly, roughly every two to seven years, and involve linked changes across the Pacific. Patterns like this are not evident at small spatial or short temporal scales, so long, widespread records were needed.

questions.stem: During El Niño, fisheries off the coast of Peru often decline. Why?
options: Stronger trade winds increase upwelling, so the water becomes too cold for fish
Heavy rain over the ocean dilutes the seawater so that marine fish cannot survive
Warm water carries extra nutrients, so plankton grow too quickly for fish to eat
Weaker trade winds reduce the upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water along the coast
questions.explanation: Upwelling brings nutrients to the surface, supporting plankton and fish. When the trades weaken, a layer of warm, nutrient-poor water covers the coast and productivity falls.

questions.stem: For six months the SOI has been about −15 and central Pacific sea-surface temperatures have been about 1 °C above average. What is the most reasonable outlook for eastern Australia?
options: A higher chance of below-average rainfall, as these data indicate El Niño
A higher chance of above-average rainfall, as these data indicate La Niña
A certain drought, because El Niño always causes drought everywhere
No change at all, because Pacific conditions do not affect Australia
questions.explanation: A strongly negative SOI with warm central Pacific water indicates El Niño, which increases the chance of drier conditions in eastern Australia. It shifts the odds but does not guarantee drought.
